title: Chapter 85 — The Fountain
paragraphs: That for six thousand years — and no one knows how many millions of ages before — the great whales should have been spouting all over the sea, sprinkling and misting the gardens of the deep as if with so many watering-cans and misting-pots; and that for some centuries now, thousands of hunters should have been close by the whale's fountain, watching these sprinklings and spoutings — that all this should be so, and yet that down to this blessed minute (fifteen and a quarter minutes past one in the afternoon of this sixteenth day of December, A.D. 1851) it should still remain an open question whether these spoutings are, after all, really water or nothing but vapor — this is surely a remarkable thing.

Let us, then, look into this matter, along with some interesting related points. Everyone knows that, by the peculiar ingenuity of their gills, the finny tribes in general breathe the air that is always mixed into the element they swim in; so a herring or a cod might live a century without once raising its head above the surface. But because of his distinctive internal structure, which gives him real lungs like a human being's, the whale can live only by breathing the free air of the open atmosphere. Hence his need to visit the upper world at regular intervals. But he cannot breathe through his mouth at all, for in his ordinary posture the Sperm Whale's mouth is buried at least eight feet below the surface; and, what is more, his windpipe has no connection with his mouth. No, he breathes through his spiracle, or blowhole, alone; and this is on the top of his head.

If I say that in any creature breathing is only a function indispensable to life, in that it draws from the air a certain element which, once brought into contact with the blood, gives the blood its life-giving principle, I don't think I shall be wrong — though I may be using some unnecessary scientific words. Assume it, and it follows that if all the blood in a man could be aerated with one breath, he might then seal up his nostrils and not take another for a considerable time. That is to say, he would then live without breathing. Strange as it may seem, this is exactly the case with the whale, who systematically lives, at intervals, his full hour and more (when at the bottom) without drawing a single breath or inhaling so much as a particle of air in any way; for remember, he has no gills. How is this? Between his ribs and on each side of his spine he is supplied with a remarkable, intricate Cretan labyrinth of vermicelli-like vessels, and when he leaves the surface these vessels are completely swollen with oxygenated blood. So for an hour or more, a thousand fathoms down in the sea, he carries a surplus stock of vitality in him, just as the camel crossing the waterless desert carries a surplus supply of drink for future use in its four supplementary stomachs. The anatomical fact of this labyrinth is indisputable; and that the supposition founded on it is reasonable and true seems all the more convincing to me when I consider that leviathan's otherwise inexplicable stubbornness in "having his spoutings out," as the fishermen put it. This is what I mean. If undisturbed, the Sperm Whale, on rising to the surface, will stay there for a length of time exactly the same as on all his other undisturbed risings. Say he stays eleven minutes and jets seventy times — that is, takes seventy breaths; then whenever he rises again, he is sure to take his seventy breaths over again, to the minute. Now, if after he has taken a few breaths you alarm him so that he sounds, he will keep dodging back up to make good his regular allowance of air. And not until those seventy breaths are counted out will he finally go down to stay out his full term below. Notice, however, that these rates differ from one whale to another; but in any one whale they are the same. Now, why should the whale insist like this on having his spoutings out, unless it is to refill his reservoir of air before descending for good? How obvious it is, too, that this necessity of rising exposes the whale to all the fatal hazards of the chase. For neither hook nor net could catch this vast leviathan when he is sailing a thousand fathoms beneath the sunlight. So it is not so much your skill, O hunter, as these great necessities that win you the victory!

In man, breathing goes on incessantly — one breath serving for only two or three heartbeats; so whatever other business he has to attend to, waking or sleeping, breathe he must, or die he will. But the Sperm Whale breathes only about one-seventh of his time — his Sunday, so to speak.

It has been said that the whale breathes only through his spout-hole. If it could truthfully be added that his spouts are mixed with water, then I think we would have the reason why his sense of smell seems wiped out in him; for the only thing about him that at all corresponds to a nose is that same spout-hole, and being so clogged with two elements, it could hardly be expected to have the power of smelling. But because of the mystery of the spout — whether it is water or whether it is vapor — no absolute certainty can yet be reached on this point. It is certain, nevertheless, that the Sperm Whale has no proper organs of smell. But what does he want them for? There are no roses, no violets, no cologne in the sea.

Furthermore, since his windpipe opens only into the tube of his spouting canal, and since that long canal — like the grand Erie Canal — is fitted with a sort of locks (which open and shut) to keep air in below or keep water out above, the whale has no voice; unless you insult him by saying that when he rumbles so strangely, he is talking through his nose. But then again, what has the whale to say? I have seldom known any profound being that had anything to say to this world, unless forced to stammer out something to earn a living. Oh, how lucky that the world is such an excellent listener!

Now, the Sperm Whale's spouting canal, meant chiefly as it is for carrying air, runs for several feet horizontally just beneath the upper surface of his head, and a little to one side; this curious canal is very much like a gas-pipe laid down on one side of a city street. But the question comes back whether this gas-pipe is also a water-pipe; in other words, whether the Sperm Whale's spout is merely the vapor of the exhaled breath, or whether that exhaled breath is mixed with water taken in at the mouth and discharged through the spiracle. It is certain that the mouth connects indirectly with the spouting canal; but it cannot be proved that this is for the purpose of discharging water through the spiracle. For the greatest need to do so would seem to arise when he accidentally takes in water while feeding. But the Sperm Whale's food is far beneath the surface, and there he cannot spout even if he wanted to. Besides, if you watch him very closely and time him with your watch, you will find that, when he is undisturbed, there is an unvarying rhythm between the timing of his jets and his ordinary periods of breathing.

But why bother anyone with all this reasoning about it? Just say it plainly! You have seen him spout, so tell us what the spout is. Can't you tell water from air? My dear sir, in this world these plain things are not so easy to settle. I have always found the plain things the most tangled of all. And as for this whale spout, you could almost stand in it and still not be sure exactly what it is.

The central body of it is hidden in the snowy, sparkling mist that envelops it; and how can you tell for certain whether any water falls from it, when, whenever you are near enough to a whale to get a close view of his spout, he is always in a tremendous commotion, with the water cascading all around him? And if at such times you thought you really saw drops of moisture in the spout, how do you know that they are not merely condensed from its vapor? Or how do you know that they are not those very drops lying on the surface of the spout-hole fissure, which is countersunk into the top of the whale's head? For even when he is swimming tranquilly through the midday sea in a calm, with his raised hump as sun-dried as a dromedary's in the desert — even then the whale always carries a small basin of water on his head, just as under a blazing sun you will sometimes see a hollow in a rock filled up with rain.

Nor is it at all wise for the hunter to be too curious about the precise nature of the whale's spout. It won't do for him to go peering into it and putting his face in it. You cannot go to this fountain with your pitcher, fill it, and carry it away. For even slight contact with the outer, vapory shreds of the jet, which will often happen, makes your skin smart feverishly from the acrid sting of the stuff that touches it. And I know a man who came into still closer contact with the spout — whether with some scientific object in view or otherwise, I cannot say — and the skin peeled off his cheek and arm. So among whalemen the spout is considered poisonous; they try to avoid it. Another thing: I have heard it said, and I don't much doubt it, that if the jet is spouted straight into your eyes, it will blind you. The wisest thing the investigator can do, then, it seems to me, is to leave this deadly spout alone.

Still, we can form a hypothesis, even if we cannot prove and establish it. My hypothesis is this: that the spout is nothing but mist. And besides other reasons, I am driven to this conclusion by considerations of the great inherent dignity and sublimity of the Sperm Whale. I consider him no common, shallow being, since it is an undisputed fact that he is never found on soundings — in water shallow enough to reach bottom with a lead line — or near shores; all other whales sometimes are. He is both ponderous and profound. And I am convinced that from the heads of all ponderous, profound beings, such as Plato, Pyrrho, the Devil, Jupiter, Dante, and so on, there always rises a certain half-visible steam while they are thinking deep thoughts. While I was composing a little treatise on Eternity, I had the curiosity to set a mirror in front of me; and before long I saw reflected there a curious, intricate worming and rippling in the air over my head. The invariable dampness of my hair while I am plunged in deep thought, after six cups of hot tea in my thin-shingled attic on an August noon — this seems a further argument for the above supposition.

And how grandly it lifts our idea of the mighty, misty monster to see him sailing solemnly through a calm tropical sea, his vast, gentle head overhung by a canopy of vapor produced by his incommunicable thoughts — and that vapor, as you will sometimes see, glorified by a rainbow, as if Heaven itself had set its seal on his thinking. For, you see, rainbows do not come to clear air; they light up only vapor. And in the same way, through all the thick mists of dim doubt in my mind, divine intuitions shoot every now and then, lighting up my fog with a heavenly ray. And I thank God for it; for everyone has doubts, and many deny, but few who have doubts or denials have intuitions along with them. Doubts about all things earthly and intuitions of some things heavenly — this combination makes neither believer nor infidel, but makes a man who looks on both with an even eye.
